what.text: Tesofensine is a small-molecule drug taken by mouth, not a peptide. It blocks the reuptake of three brain chemicals: noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin. That makes it a "triple reuptake inhibitor".

src.label: Astrup et al., tesofensine phase 2, Lancet

what.text: It was first tested for Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease. Weight loss in those trials led to its testing for obesity. Tesomet is a combination of tesofensine with metoprolol, a heart-rate-lowering drug, tested in rare forms of obesity.

research.text: The published human evidence is a handful of Phase 2 and smaller studies. There is no published Phase 3 trial in PubMed or on ClinicalTrials.gov. The main studies are listed below as they were run.

research.title: Phase 2: weight in adults with obesity

facts.v: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, five Danish obesity centers
203 adults with a BMI of 30 to 40, all on a reduced-calorie diet
daily tesofensine 0.25, 0.5 or 1.0 mg, or placebo

research.found: Weight fell by 2.0% on placebo and 4.5%, 9.2% and 10.6% on the three tesofensine doses. 79% finished the study. Dry mouth, nausea, constipation, diarrhea and trouble sleeping were the most common side effects. Heart rate rose by 7.4 beats per minute on 0.5 mg. The authors said the findings needed confirming in Phase 3. In 2013, The Lancet published an expression of concern about this paper, and the authors replied in a letter titled "Under-reporting of adverse effects of tesofensine". ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00394667.

research.title: Tesomet in hypothalamic obesity

facts.v: tesofensine 0.5 mg with metoprolol 50 mg, or placebo, with diet advice
safety (main goal); weight, appetite and quality of life

research.found: 18 people finished. Compared with placebo, weight changed by a further -6.3%. One person had a serious worsening of anxiety linked to the drug and stopped. Sleep problems (50% vs 13%), dry mouth (43% vs 0%) and headache (36% vs 0%) were more common on Tesomet. Heart rate and blood pressure did not differ between groups.

src.label: Huynh et al., Tesomet in hypothalamic obesity, Eur J Endocrinol

research.title: Abuse potential in recreational stimulant users

facts.v: tesofensine, placebo, d-amphetamine, bupropion or atomoxetine, one at a time
drug liking and other abuse-related effects

research.found: Tesofensine’s effects did not differ from placebo on the main measures and were lower than d-amphetamine’s. The authors concluded its abuse potential was no greater than that of bupropion or atomoxetine.

src.label: Schoedel et al., abuse-potential study, Clin Pharmacol Ther

research.text: A pooled analysis of 4 trials, each 14 weeks long, in Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease (740 people on tesofensine, 228 on placebo, no diet program) found weight changes of -0.5% to -2.8% on tesofensine, depending on dose, versus +0.5% on placebo. Heart rate rose by up to 6.8 beats per minute; blood pressure did not change.

research.text: A 2007 to 2008 long-term safety study of tesofensine in 140 people with obesity is listed as completed on ClinicalTrials.gov. The search found no journal report of its results.

research.text: In diet-induced obese rats, 14 days of tesofensine lowered food intake and body weight and changed dopamine levels in brain reward areas. Those findings come from animals.
